candidates.statement: Differences in physiology between females and males can lead to differences in disease 86 manifestations, as well as differences in the pharmacokinetics (PK), pharmacodynamics (PD), 87 efficacy, and safety of medical products (Madla 2021). Consequently, it is important to 88 characterize the impact of sex as part of medical product development to determine if there may 89 be differences in PK, PD, effectiveness, and/or safety associated with use of the medical product. 90 Identification of a clinically relevant difference by sex may inform a benefit-risk assessment and 91 inform product labeling. Assessment of sex differences should occur throughout drug 92

candidates.statement: Sponsors should evaluate whether the demographic distribution of the potential trial population 132 changes across different key time points (e.g., at screening, including evaluation of trial 133 inclusion/exclusion criteria; after consent; and at various follow-up time points) and whether 134 these changes have an impact on trial participation. For example, if the proportion of females 135 drops significantly after screening for inclusion/exclusion criteria, this may suggest a need to 136 reexamine the inclusion/exclusion criteria. Removing or limiting unnecessary criteria could 137 improve the participation rates of females in the trial. Sponsors should also consider consulting 138 with academic institutions, health organizations that focus on female health (including 139 community-based organizations), and contract research organizations to determine practices best 140 suited to reducing challenges in enrollment and retention. Sponsors should also engage with the 141 patient community to help develop strategies for addressing enrollment and retention 142 challenges. 21

candidates.statement: For most drugs and devices, males and females should be included in clinical trials in numbers 179 adequate to allow for reliable benefit-risk assessments and to understand any potential sex- 180 related differences in medical product response. Sponsors should consider the following 181 recommendations: 182

• In a trial where there may be a plausible biological reason to expect a different response 184 in females and males to the medical product, the numbers of females and males 185 representing the prevalence/incidence of the disease or condition may not be sufficient to 186 evaluate a sex difference in medical product safety or efficacy. Where sex differences 187 are anticipated, there should be sufficient numbers to inform reliable benefit-risk 188 assessments in males and females. 28 Sponsors should consult with the appropriate FDA 189 review division to consider target enrollment of female and male participants. candidates.statement: Analyzing sex differences in medical product performance is an important component of 236 assessing product safety and effectiveness and can inform what goes in the product labeling to 237 improve patient care. Analyzing sex differences may involve (1) characterizing the treatment 238 effects for females and for males and any clinically relevant differences or potential differences 239 in those treatment effects, (2) determining whether the product provides greater benefits or risks 240 for a particular sex, (3) determining whether particular benefits or risks exist only for a particular 241 sex, or (4) determining how relevant the treatment effect for a particular sex is to understanding 242 the treatment effect for another sex. Apparent sex differences may result in the need to mitigate 243 clinically significant differences in safety or effectiveness between females and males. 244
candidates.context: The optimal analysis approach will depend on the type of inference that is sought. For example, 246 different approaches may be appropriate for characterizing potential differences in treatment 247 effects between sexes in contrast to estimating the treatment effect within a given sex. Sex is one 248 of many potential demographic characteristics typically evaluated in subgroup analyses of a 249 clinical trial or non-interventional study. When many subgroup analyses are performed, some of 250 the estimated treatment effects may represent random highs and random lows, being far above or 251 far below the respective underlying subgroup treatment effect. Observed differential treatment 252

candidates.statement: In general, sponsors should plan and conduct analyses to evaluate and understand potential 257 heterogeneity of treatment effects by sex on key effectiveness and safety endpoints. This should 258 include analyses for differences in treatment effects and to estimate treatment effects in females 259 and males. Considerations and recommendations related to these two different types of analyses 260 are provided in sections IV.B and C below. In many cases, it may be beneficial to conduct 261 analyses for individual trials or studies but also combine results across similarly designed trials 262 and studies. Analyses of integrated data from multiple trials or studies should stratify by trial or 263 study. Such analyses may have greater precision and power than analyses of individual trials and 264 studies and may be appropriate if meaningful differences in treatment effects are not expected 265 across trials and studies. 266

candidates.statement: Analyses to evaluate differences in treatment effects between females and males should include 270 calculation of an estimated difference in treatment effects, along with associated uncertainty 271 (e.g., a 95% confidence interval (CI) for the difference). Such analyses can also include a test 272 for a quantitative interaction of treatment by sex (i.e., a test for whether the treatment effect is 273 larger for females or for males (the two-sided alternative hypothesis) or whether those treatment 274 effects are similar (the null hypothesis)). 275
candidates.context: B. Analyses for Differences in Treatment Effects Between Females and Males 268 Unless the clinical trial or study provides statistical power near 100% for demonstrating a 277 positive average treatment effect in the overall population (which is unlikely), statistical tests for 278 detecting plausible magnitudes of differences in treatment effects by sex (i.e., tests of a 279 treatment-by-sex interaction) tend to be underpowered. The 95% CI for the difference in 280 treatment effects by sex may be very wide and may include large differences. In many cases, the 281 test for a treatment-by-sex interaction may only have sufficient power to detect large differences 282 in treatment effects by sex. There may be insufficient power for some smaller, but still clinically 283 important, differences in treatment effects by sex. Therefore, lack of statistical significance 284 when testing for differ

candidates.statement: Analyses should be planned and conducted to estimate treatment effects and corresponding 300 uncertainty (i.e., a 95% CI) in females and males. Traditionally, only data from a given sex have 301 been used when estimating the treatment effect size for that sex. Sponsors should consider 302 prespecified statistical approaches that incorporate the data from all participants when estimating 303 the treatment effect within a given sex. For example, the relevance of the data from males in 304 estimating the treatment effect for females depends on how similar the results from males are to 305 the results from females and how much data there are for females alone. Estimators of sex- 306 specific treatment effects have greater precision than estimators based solely on the data for a 307 given sex (Pennello 2018). As noted earlier, sex is only one of many factors for which subgroup 308 analyses are typically performed, such that subgroup estimated treatment effects are subject to 309 random highs and lows, being far above or far below the respective underlying subgroup 310 treatment effect. Prespecified statistical approaches, which can also simultaneously consider 311 multiple factors, should quantitatively address these random highs and lows and can reduce the 312 potential for misinterpretation and making incorrect decisions resulting from those 313 misinterpretations (Lipsky 2010). 314

Reporting Results of Analyses 316 Because the enrollment demographics of the clinical study may impact the generalizability of the 322 conclusions, for clinical studies of devices, FDA recommends that sponsors report the number 323 and proportion of study participants by sex who were treated or diagnosed with the device as part 324 of a clinical study as appropriate. Where statistical significance is achieved for an average 325 treatment effect for the overall population, the results for each subgroup by sex should be 326 examined to understand whether the finding for the overall population was driven by the results 327 in only one of the sexes. Any potential difference by sex should be investigated, explained, and 328 discussed with the Agency. 329

Considerations if Differences in Treatment Effects Between Females and 341 Males Are Anticipated at the Design Stage 342 When a clinically important treatment effect is more likely for one sex than another sex, an 349 early-phase trial (e.g., phase 1 or phase 2) should ideally be performed to obtain information on 350 differences by sex. If there is evidence of benefit from the early-phase trials for a particular sex 351 and uncertainty around benefit for another sex, pivotal trials 37 can be designed to establish 352 benefit for the sex for which there is evidence of benefit and also continue to study the effects of 353 the product for the sex in which there is uncertainty around the benefit. 354

candidates.statement: In such a setting, where there is biological plausibility for benefit in a given sex and uncertainty 356 around benefit for another sex, a trial can include certain approaches to control the type I error 357 probability across testing in the overall population and testing separately within a given sex. 358 Such testing schemes are used due to concerns that adding data from the sex for which there is 359 large uncertainty around benefit to the data from the sex for which there is expectation of benefit 360 will reduce the probability of a statistically significant finding. With such an approach, if 361 statistical significance is achieved only for the sex where there was expectation of benefit, then 362 performing a statistical test after adding the data from another sex will only be capable of 363 determining whether there is evidence of an average treatment effect in the overall population. 364 The test in the overall population may be driven by results in the sex where benefit was expected 365 and does not identify a treatment effect within the sex for which there was uncertainty around 366 benefit. The estimated treatment effect and the estimated treatment effect’s reliability would 367 need to be considered before determining whether there is benefit for the sex for which benefit 368 was uncertain. 369
